glossary.example: The Shungas added carved railings to the Bharhut Stupa.

glossary.definition: Writing carved into stone, metal or other lasting material, often recording a ruler's deeds, gifts or beliefs.
glossary.example: The Hathigumpha inscription records King Kharavela's accomplishments year after year.

glossary.definition: The oldest literature of south India: anthologies of Tamil poems expressing love, heroism and generosity, which gave the 'Sangam Age' its name.
glossary.example: Historians consult Sangam literature to understand ancient southern society.

glossary.definition: A style of architecture in which rooms, pillars, shrines and sculptures are carved directly out of solid rock.
glossary.example: The Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves and the Karla caves are examples of rock-cut architecture.

glossary.definition: A network of ancient trade routes connecting China with the Mediterranean world, passing through Central Asia and Persia.
glossary.example: The Kushanas controlled significant sections of the Silk Route, so trade grew.

glossary.definition: The flowing together and blending of different cultures to create new shared styles, while keeping a dominant local character.
glossary.example: Gandhara art is a confluence of Greco-Roman and Indian styles.

glossary.definition: A counted era or calendar that begins from a fixed event; from Sanskrit saṃvatsara ('year').
glossary.example: The Shaka Samvat, which began in 78 CE, is India's official national calendar.

glossary.definition: A low dam built across a river to raise the water and divert it into canals; from Tamil aṇai ('dam') + kaṭṭu ('to build').
glossary.example: The Chola Grand Anicut (Kallanai) is one of the oldest dams still in use.

glossary.definition: Someone who supports artists, builders or a religion with money and protection; from Latin patronus ('protector').
glossary.example: Kanishka was a great patron of Buddhism and of Gandhara and Mathura art.

glossary.definition: A Greco-Buddhist style of art from the northwest that gave Buddhist subjects Hellenistic (Greek/Roman) forms, such as wavy hair and toga-like robes.
glossary.example: A Gandhara Buddha can look almost like a Greek statue.

glossary.definition: An indigenous Indian art style centred on Mathura that carved the Buddha and other figures in spotted red sandstone with fuller, rounder forms.
glossary.example: The Mathura school worked in distinctive red sandstone.

glossary.definition: A long stretch of history counted from a fixed starting point or event; from Latin aera ('a number used for reckoning').
glossary.example: The Shaka era and the Common Era count years from different starting points.

miniProjects.title: Design a coin like an ancient king
needs: A circle of cardboard or air-dry clay
A pencil, toothpick or blunt nail to carve
Reference pictures of Satavahana, Indo-Greek and Kushana coins
steps: Choose which kingdom you are a ruler of — Satavahana, Indo-Greek, Chera, or Kushana.
On one face, design a 'royal' side: your portrait or a symbol, plus a title (like 'King of Kings').
On the other face, choose an emblem or deity that shows your kingdom's values — a ship for sea trade, a deity for your faith, an animal emblem.
Carve or draw both sides onto your cardboard or clay disc.
Add a short inscription in block letters around the edge, the way Brahmi or Greek script ran around real coins.
Paint it to look like gold, silver or copper.
Write three sentences explaining what your coin would tell a future historian about your kingdom.
miniProjects.expectedObservation: You will discover that a tiny coin can carry a king's name, faith, trade and values all at once — which is exactly why historians treat ancient coins as treasure-troves of evidence.
miniProjects.whyItWorks: Real Satavahana, Indo-Greek and Kushana coins are among the main sources historians use, because rulers deliberately chose what to stamp on them. By designing your own, you experience first-hand how images and inscriptions encode a whole society.

miniProjects.title: Build the Age of Reorganisation timeline
needs: A long sheet of paper or a roll of chart paper
steps: Draw a long horizontal line. Mark '200 BCE' at the left and '300 CE' at the right, with '0' (the BCE-to-CE turn) in the middle.
Mark 185 BCE — the assassination of the last Maurya emperor by Pushyamitra Shunga.
Add the dynasties as coloured bars where they ruled: Shungas, Chedis, Satavahanas, Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Kushanas, and the southern Cholas-Cheras-Pandyas.
Place the key rulers above their dynasty's bar: Pushyamitra Shunga, Kharavela, Gautamiputra Satakarni, Karikala, Kanishka.
Mark the transition point from BCE to CE and write how the counting changes there.
Count and write down how many years the whole period covers, from the first year of the 2nd century BCE to the last year of the 3rd century CE.
Decorate each dynasty with a tiny symbol — a ship for the Satavahanas, a horse for the ashvamedha, a coin for the Kushanas.
miniProjects.expectedObservation: You will see at a glance that several dynasties ruled at the SAME time in different regions, and how the period bridges the BCE-to-CE divide — making the 'reorganisation' of the map visible.
miniProjects.whyItWorks: Laying overlapping dynasties on one line shows that history is not a single line of kings but many parallel stories. Marking the BCE-CE turn reinforces how historians measure time, just as the textbook's 'Let's Remember' box asks.

whatIfs.question: What if the last Maurya emperor had not been assassinated in 185 BCE?
whatIfs.answer: If the Mauryan line had stayed strong, the empire might have held its provinces together for longer, and the political 'reorganisation' into many competing kingdoms could have been delayed. A strong central power would also have kept the northwest frontier well defended, making it much harder for the Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushanas to enter. We might then have seen far less of the rich cultural blending — the Gandhara art, the syncretic coins of Kanishka — that grew precisely because many kingdoms and incoming peoples met and mixed. The fragmentation, though it brought conflict, was also what made the great cultural confluence of this age possible.

whatIfs.question: What if we had no coins or inscriptions from this period?
whatIfs.answer: We would know far less about the Age of Reorganisation. So much of our knowledge comes from physical evidence: Satavahana coins showing ships prove their sea trade; Indo-Greek coins, found in excavations, give us most of what we know about those rulers; Kanishka's coins reveal his titles and the gods he honoured; and inscriptions like the Hathigumpha and the Nashik and Naneghat records tell us about Kharavela and powerful Satavahana queens. Without these durable sources, the rulers, religions, trade and even the role of women in this age would be almost a blank — showing how vital coins and inscriptions are to historians.

timelines.title: The Age of Reorganisation: from 185 BCE to the 3rd century CE
timelines.intro: A chronological walk through the key rulers and dynasties of the post-Maurya age, crossing from BCE into CE. Notice how several kingdoms ruled at the same time in different parts of the subcontinent.

steps.label: c. 185 BCE — Maurya breakup
steps.body: The last Maurya emperor is assassinated by his commander-in-chief, Pushyamitra Shunga, who founds the Shunga dynasty over north and central India.

steps.label: 2nd century BCE — Satavahanas rise
steps.body: The Satavahanas come to rule large parts of the Deccan, building wealth on the Krishna-Godavari farmland and on sea trade reaching Rome.

steps.label: 2nd century BCE — Indo-Greeks
steps.body: Indo-Greek rulers, descended from Alexander's satraps, take the weakened northwest and blend Greek and Indian culture.

steps.label: 1st century BCE — Kharavela of Kalinga
steps.body: The Chedi king Kharavela, the Jain 'monk-king', records his deeds in the Hathigumpha inscription near Bhubaneswar.

steps.label: Late 2nd c. BCE–5th c. CE — Shakas
steps.body: The Shakas (Indo-Scythians) replace the Indo-Greeks; the Shaka Samvat calendar is developed during their period.

steps.label: 2nd century CE — Kushanas & Kanishka
steps.body: The Central Asian Kushanas, peaking under Kanishka, control the Silk Route; Gandhara and Mathura art flourish.

steps.label: 2nd c. BCE–3rd c. CE — Sangam Age (South)
steps.body: In the south the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas flourish; Sangam Tamil poetry defines the era. Karikala builds the Grand Anicut.

steps.label: 3rd century CE — Satavahanas fragment
steps.body: The Satavahana Empire breaks into smaller kingdoms due to weak central control and economic decline, opening the way for new regional powers.

examConnections.title: Post-Maurya kingdoms return in later classes
examConnections.body: The Shungas, Satavahanas, Kushanas, Sangam kingdoms and the Indo-Greek/Shaka invasions reappear in much more detail in Class 11-12 History and in competitive exams. Topics like Indo-Roman trade, the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art, Kanishka and the spread of Buddhism along the Silk Route, and the Sangam Age are favourites in UPSC, NTSE and state PSC papers. Mastering the simple version now — who ruled where, what each is famous for — makes the advanced version far easier later.

examConnections.title: Coins and inscriptions as sources
examConnections.body: This chapter is a perfect case study in 'sources of history' — a theme examiners love. Satavahana ship-coins, Indo-Greek bilingual coins, Kanishka's coins, and inscriptions like the Hathigumpha, Nashik and Naneghat records all show how historians reconstruct the past from physical evidence. Olympiad and quiz questions often ask which dynasty issued a described coin or what a named inscription tells us, so practise linking each ruler to their distinctive source.

deepDive.title: Indo-Roman trade and the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
deepDive.body: The Satavahana, Chera and Pandya trade with Rome is documented not only by Indian coins but by a remarkable Greek sailing manual, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, written in the 1st century CE. It lists Indian ports, the goods bought and sold there, and even the best sailing seasons using the monsoon winds. Indian exports of pepper, pearls, ivory and textiles drew so much Roman gold that the Roman writer Pliny complained India was draining Rome's treasury. Large hoards of Roman coins found in south India confirm this. Studying these sources together shows how historians cross-check different kinds of evidence — foreign texts, local coins and archaeology — to reconstruct ancient trade.
deepDive.prerequisite: Knowing the Cheras, Pandyas and Satavahanas traded with the Roman Empire.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Find out what the 'monsoon winds' had to do with the timing of voyages between India and Rome.

deepDive.title: Gandhara, Mathura and the first human image of the Buddha
deepDive.body: Before the Kushana period, the Buddha was usually shown only by symbols — a footprint, an empty seat, a wheel — never as a person (the 'aniconic' style seen at Bharhut). It was in the Gandhara and Mathura schools, under the Kushanas, that the Buddha first began to be carved in human form. Gandhara, drawing on Greco-Roman art, gave him a realistic, draped, almost classical look in grey schist; Mathura, drawing on the older Indian yaksha tradition, gave him a fuller, energetic form in red sandstone. The move to human-form deities here is one of the great turning points in Indian art, and it 'laid the groundwork' for the deity sculptures of later Hindu and Buddhist temples.
deepDive.prerequisite: Understanding the difference between the Gandhara and Mathura schools.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Look up an 'aniconic' Bharhut relief and compare it with a Gandhara Buddha image.

crossChapterRefs.pointer: This chapter begins exactly where the Maurya chapter ends — with the assassination of Ashoka's last successor around 185 BCE. The Kalinga war and Ashoka's edicts mentioned here connect directly back to the previous chapter on the Mauryas.

The geography learnt earlier explains this age: the fertile Krishna-Godavari and Kaveri deltas fed the Satavahanas and Cholas, while long coastlines and ports made the sea trade of the Cheras and Pandyas with Rome possible.

bossQuestions.prompt: Who assassinated the last Maurya emperor around 185 BCE?
solutionSteps: Recall the Maurya breakup around 185 BCE.
The commander-in-chief who did it founded the Shunga dynasty.
That was Pushyamitra Shunga.
commonMistakes: Confusing him with Kanishka (Kushana) or Kharavela (Chedi).

bossQuestions.prompt: Which ritual did Pushyamitra Shunga perform to declare himself a powerful ruler?
solutionSteps: Recall the Vedic horse ritual used to declare kingship.
It is the ashvamedha yajna.
commonMistakes: Confusing the ritual with the Silk Route (a trade route) or Sangam (a poets' assembly).

bossQuestions.prompt: Satavahana coins often depict ships, which best suggests that the kingdom —
options: Was at constant war with the Shungas
solutionSteps: A ship on official coinage points to seafaring trade.
Satavahana coins with ships were found on both coasts.
commonMistakes: Reading the ship as religious rather than commercial.

bossQuestions.prompt: The Satavahana king Gautamiputra Satakarni was named after his —
solutionSteps: 'Gautamiputra' means 'son of Gautami'.
Satavahana princes were often named after their mothers.
commonMistakes: Assuming kings were named after fathers.

bossQuestions.prompt: The Hathigumpha inscription near Bhubaneswar records the deeds of which ruler?
solutionSteps: The Hathigumpha inscription is in the Udayagiri caves of Kalinga.
It records the Chedi king Kharavela's accomplishments year by year.
commonMistakes: Confusing Kharavela with the Chola Karikala or the Kushana Kanishka.

bossQuestions.prompt: Which Chola king built the Kallanai or Grand Anicut on the Kaveri?
solutionSteps: Recall the Chola king famed for public works.
Karikala built the Grand Anicut to irrigate the Kaveri delta.
commonMistakes: Attributing the dam to a non-Chola ruler.

bossQuestions.prompt: The three crowned kingdoms of the south whose poets created the Sangam literature were the —
solutionSteps: Recall the three southern 'crowned kings'.
They were the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas.
commonMistakes: Mixing southern kingdoms with northern or invading dynasties.

bossQuestions.prompt: The Shaka Samvat calendar is how many years behind the Gregorian calendar?
solutionSteps: The Shaka calendar was developed in the Shaka period.
It runs 78 years behind the Gregorian calendar.
commonMistakes: Confusing it with the Vikram Samvat (57 years) or with the adoption year 1957.

bossQuestions.prompt: The Gandhara school of art is best described as —
options: A purely Indian style in red sandstone
A blend of Greco-Roman and Indian styles, mostly in grey schist
bossQuestions.answer: A blend of Greco-Roman and Indian styles, mostly in grey schist
solutionSteps: Gandhara arose in the Greek-influenced northwest (Punjab region).
It blended Greco-Roman and Indian features in grey-black schist.
commonMistakes: Confusing Gandhara (grey schist, Greco-Roman) with Mathura (red sandstone, Indian).

bossQuestions.prompt: The chapter's big idea is best summed up by which phrase?
options: A dark age of total decline
A tapestry of the past — confluence amid conflict
Conquest by foreign rulers who erased Indian culture
A single empire ruling all of India
bossQuestions.answer: A tapestry of the past — confluence amid conflict
solutionSteps: The chapter stresses cultural exchange alongside political conflict.
It frames the age as a 'tapestry' woven from many threads, with Indian themes dominant.
commonMistakes: Reading the age as pure decline or as cultural erasure.

bossQuestions.prompt: Besides warfare, the new kingdoms of this age often gained territory PEACEFULLY by —
solutionSteps: Recall the two ways kingdoms gained territory.
One was warfare; the other was matrimonial alliances.
Royal marriages joined families and lands peacefully.
commonMistakes: Assuming all territory was won only by war.

bossQuestions.prompt: The Shungas are especially remembered for adding beautifully carved railings and reliefs to which famous monument?
solutionSteps: Recall the Shungas patronised art and architecture.
Their most famous work was the carved railings of the Bharhut Stupa.
It lies in present-day Madhya Pradesh.
commonMistakes: Confusing the Bharhut Stupa with the Chola Grand Anicut or Ashoka's Sarnath pillar.

bossQuestions.prompt: The Gandhara AND Mathura schools of art both flourished under the patronage of which dynasty?
solutionSteps: Both great art schools arose at the same time.
They flourished under the Kushanas.
Gandhara blended Greco-Roman and Indian styles; Mathura was distinctly Indian.
commonMistakes: Crediting the Indo-Greeks — the two schools peaked under the Kushanas.

quickCheckQuestions.prompt: The period after the Maurya breakup is called the 'Age of Reorganisation' because —
options: A single new empire reorganised all of India
Regions were rearranged into many new competing kingdoms
The northwest became the strongest region
quickCheckQuestions.answer: Regions were rearranged into many new competing kingdoms
solutionSteps: The empire broke into many kingdoms.
These competed to grow, rearranging the political map.
commonMistakes: Thinking one empire reorganised everything.

quickCheckQuestions.prompt: An Indo-Greek ambassador set up the Heliodorus pillar praising which Indian god?
solutionSteps: The Heliodorus pillar inscription praises Vasudeva as the 'god of gods'.
Vasudeva is another name for Krishna.
commonMistakes: Picking another deity mentioned elsewhere in the chapter.

quickCheckQuestions.prompt: Which dynasty controlled significant sections of the Silk Route, helping trade grow?
solutionSteps: The Central Asian Kushanas held parts of the Silk Route.
Under them, trade grew, linking India with Asia and the West.
commonMistakes: Confusing the Kushanas with southern or northern Indian dynasties.

quickCheckQuestions.prompt: King Kharavela of Kalinga, who left the Hathigumpha inscription, was a devoted follower of which teachings?
solutionSteps: Recall the Chedi ruler Kharavela of Kalinga.
He was a devoted follower of Jain teachings.
His deeds are recorded in the Hathigumpha inscription.
commonMistakes: Confusing Kharavela's faith with the foreign cultures of the northwest invaders.

quickCheckQuestions.prompt: Compared with the Greco-Roman-influenced Gandhara school, the Mathura school of art had a style that was distinctly —
solutionSteps: Two art schools arose under the Kushanas.
Gandhara blended Greco-Roman and Indian features.
Mathura's style was distinctly Indian.
commonMistakes: Mixing up Mathura (Indian style) with Gandhara (blended style).
